newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy to crack down on privileges to Mob turncoats.
newsitem.headline: Italy to crack down on privileges to Mob turncoats.

text.p: Italy's government has drawn up a draft law aimed at overhauling the witness protection programme for Mafia turncoats, who have been accused of using state money to lead lives of luxury.
Newspapers reported on Saturday that the government had approved a bill that would introduce key changes to the privileged treatment normally reserved for mobsters who turn state's evidence.

"We're convinced this law, which we hope parliament will pass quickly...meets the needs of magistrates involved in the anti-Mafia fight as well as the public," Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick was quoted as saying in La Stampa daily.

The proposed law, which would make it harder to become a turncoat and reduce their often exorbitant pay, comes at a time of intense debate over their privileges and the reliability of their testimony.

Many defendants on trial as a result of important turncoat evidence, including former prime minister Giulio Andreotti, argue that their accusers are lying to protect their own skins and stay out of jail.

Andreotti expressed outrage in December after a prosecution witness in a Mafia trial against him said he had received 500 million lire ($325,000) from the state in exchange for taking part in the witness protection programme.
On Friday, a witness in a separate murder trial against Andreotti told a court that investigators had put words in his mouth and fabricated evidence.

Gaetano Sangiorgi, a doctor accused of involvement in a Mafia killing, told the court that Palermo investigators had promised him he could go home and continue his profession if he spoke about Andreotti.
"I told them: 'Write what you want because I don't give a damn about Andreotti. I'll sign anything,"' Sangiorgi said.
The magistrates denied the allegations, calling them the "absurd" declarations of a man accused of Mafia involvement.
The witness protection scheme, set up after the 1992 murder of anti-Mafia judge Giovanni Falcone, has proved effective.
"Boss of bosses" Salvatore 'The Beast' Riina and a string of top mobsters were all arrested as a result of unprecedented information from gangsters who broke the Mafia's code of "omerta" or silence.
But national anti-Mafia prosecutor Pierluigi Vigna said the new law would smooth over some wrinkles in the system, which has been flooded by new participants.

Under the new law, an Interior Ministry commission would examine all requests to join the programme to determine if the gangster's testimony would be "essential" to any probes, trials or preventing any crimes.

Turncoats, who would have to serve at least a fourth of their prison terms or 10 years in the case of a life sentence, would also have to tell investigators everything they know within six months of turning state's evidence.
Many turncoats have testified over several years, giving information sporadically and only when they feel like it.

"They would also have to declare all their illegally earned income which could be sequestered and used for the maintenance of turncoats...and go to a fund for Mafia victims' relatives," Vigna told La Stampa.
Official figures show 1,244 former criminals plus relatives are covered by Italy's witness protection scheme, which costs the state some 100 billion lire ($650 million) a year.
